..
Issued at 240 PM CST Wed Nov 11 2026

A shortwave trough and its associated surface low continue to 
spiral through northeast IL and northwest IN this afternoon. 
These features have lead to the development of widespread rain 
showers across much of the area and those showers are expected 
to persist through at least 6-7 PM this evening before shifting 
east into northern and eastern IN. Recent mesoanalysis also 
shows steep mid-level lapse rates (around 6-7 C/km) and some 
modest MUCAPE present across north- central IL (areas near and 
south of the Illinois and Kankakee River Valleys) which has 
generated a couple of isolated thunderstorms. While no severe 
weather is expected, taller storm cores have been producing some
instances of pea sized hail and locally gusty winds up to 45 
mph and that threat will likely continue through early evening 
as well. 

Once the ongoing showers exit, a period of dry conditions is 
expected to develop and persist through the night for most 
locales. However, some lake enhanced rain showers are expected 
to redevelop after midnight along the western shore of Lake 
Michigan and gradually pivot into northern and northwest IN by 
daybreak Thursday morning. Given that lake effect parameters 
will still be somewhat marginal Thursday morning and the lack of
a more dominant band, the lake enhanced showers will likely be 
somewhat transient and be wobbling across northwest IN and the 
IL nearshore waters through the morning. That said, another 
upper-level shortwave is forecast to dive across northern IL 
Thursday morning which could lead to some isolated light showers
and/or sprinkles. Though, with the dry mid- level air expected 
to be in place away from the lake confidence remains low that 
any inland showers/sprinkles will actually materialize. 

By Thursday afternoon, an inverted surface trough is forecast 
to pivot across Lake Michigan and northeast IL which should pull
the ongoing lake effect/enhanced rain showers into northeast 
IL. As this occurs the lake induced instability will be 
increasing which should help the developing lake effect showers 
have some inland extent, but exactly how far inland continues to
be somewhat uncertain. Regardless, the lake effect showers will
continue to manifest into a dominant band by Thursday evening 
as the instability and convergence increases. Initially the 
dominant band will likely be near the IL-IN border as it 
organizes, but will gradually pivot into northwest IN and become
quasi-stationary as it does so. Once the band settles into 
northwest IN Thursday night it is expected to remain over the 
area through Friday night. Initially, the more shallow lake 
induced inversion and warmer temperature profile will keep rain 
as the dominant precipitation type, but as temperatures cool 
Thursday night some snow flakes may try to mix in at times. With
surface temperatures expected to be in the mid-30s (33-36F) it 
looks like any snow accumulation would be very limited (less 
than a tenth of an inch) and mainly confined to colder and 
grassy surfaces. The potential for a rain/snow mix with the lake
effect will persist off and on through Friday night but again 
with the marginal temperatures accumulations should be limited. 
Though, if snow does become the dominant precipitation type and 
persists as such for an extended period of time and/or snow 
rates approach an inch per hour, then some locally higher 
accumulations up to half an inch could materialize inland of 
Lake Michigan in northwest IN. 

Outside of the lake effect, winds will also increase on 
Thursday as a strong surface high builds into northern Great 
Lakes. This will result in northwest gusts on Thursday around 
30-35 mph with locally higher gusts in excess of 40 mph possible
near Lake Michigan. While some breezy winds will persist 
through Friday gusts should be only around 20-25 mph. 

The lake effect showers will taper from west to east in 
northwest IN late Friday night into Saturday morning leaving us 
with dry conditions through at least the middle of next week. 
Temperatures will remain seasonably cool through the weekend 
with highs in the 40s and nighttime lows in the 20s and 30s 
before rebounding towards more seasonable values (in the lower 
50s) early next week.

Yack
